report:
## Report

The evidence is suggestive but not conclusive that vegetarian diets extend life expectancy compared with meat-eating.

**Supporting evidence:** Large prospective cohorts, especially the Adventist Health Study‑2 (>96,000 participants), find vegetarians have lower all-cause mortality than non-vegetarians, with protection strongest for ischemic heart disease and more consistent in men than women (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S000291652400652X). A 2025 meta-analysis of plant-based diet indices similarly reported reduced all-cause and cause-specific mortality with greater adherence to healthful plant-based patterns (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/nutrition/articles/10.3389/fnut.2025.1518519/full).

**Conflicting/weaker evidence:** A 2021 meta-analysis focused specifically on vegetarian vs. non-vegetarian diets concluded vegetarianism reduced ischemic heart disease mortality but had **no significant effect on all-cause or cerebrovascular mortality**, and rated the certainty of evidence as low (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34611632/). An umbrella review likewise found no significant reduction in all-cause mortality for vegetarians versus omnivores (RR=0.94, CI 0.86–1.04) (https://www.academia.edu/125568561/Health_Outcomes_Associated_with_Vegetarian_Diets_An_Umbrella_Review_of_Systematic_Reviews_and_Meta_Analyses).

**Key caveats:** Nearly all data are observational, subject to the "healthy user" bias—vegetarians tend to smoke less, exercise more, and have higher socioeconomic status—making causal inference difficult. Effects also vary by sex and study population (many rely heavily on Seventh-day Adventists, a distinct health-conscious group).

**Conclusion:** There is moderate, but not strong or fully causal, evidence that vegetarian diets are associated with modestly lower mortality, driven mainly by reduced cardiovascular deaths rather than a broad all-cause longevity advantage. The claim is plausible but overstated as a definitive, universally applicable fact.
